test0.query: what is non controlling interest on balance sheet
test0.query2doc: Non-controlling interest (also called minority interest) is the portion of equity in a subsidiary that is not owned by the parent company. On consolidated financial statements, the parent presents 100% of the subsidiary’s assets and liabilities but shows the non-controlling interest as a separate line within shareholders’ equity to reflect the claim of outside owners. The non-controlling interest’s share of the subsidiary’s net income is likewise shown separately on the consolidated income statement. It is typically calculated as the percentage of the subsidiary not owned by the parent multiplied by the subsidiary’s net assets (and by its net income for profit allocation). For example, if a parent owns 80% of a subsidiary whose equity is $1,000, the non-controlling interest reported would be $200. (Measurement rules at acquisition vary: under IFRS you can measure NCI at fair value or at the proportionate share of net assets; U.S. GAAP generally measures it at fair value.)
